exam1.question: What is the typical frequency range used in diagnostic medical ultrasound?
exam1.explanation: Diagnostic medical ultrasound typically uses frequencies between 2 MHz and 15 MHz. Lower frequencies (2-5 MHz) provide better penetration for deeper structures, while higher frequencies (7-15 MHz) provide better resolution for superficial structures.

exam1.question: Which of the following best describes the piezoelectric effect?

options.text: Conversion of electrical energy to mechanical energy
Reflection of sound waves at tissue interfaces
Attenuation of ultrasound beams in tissue

exam1.explanation: The piezoelectric effect is the ability of certain materials to convert electrical energy into mechanical energy (and vice versa). This principle is fundamental to ultrasound transducers, which convert electrical signals into sound waves and returning echoes back into electrical signals.

exam1.question: What happens to spatial resolution as frequency increases?
exam1.explanation: Higher frequencies provide better spatial resolution because they produce shorter wavelengths. However, this comes at the cost of reduced penetration depth due to increased attenuation.

exam1.question: Which artifact occurs when the ultrasound beam encounters a strong reflector, causing multiple echoes?
exam1.explanation: Reverberation artifact occurs when ultrasound encounters a strong reflector and bounces back and forth between the transducer and the reflector multiple times, creating equally spaced parallel echoes.

exam1.question: What is the relationship between frequency and wavelength in ultrasound?
exam1.explanation: Frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional. As frequency increases, wavelength decreases. This relationship is described by the equation: wavelength = propagation speed / frequency.

exam1.question: What is the average propagation speed of ultrasound in soft tissue?
exam1.explanation: The average propagation speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1,540 m/s (or 1.54 mm/µs). This value is used by ultrasound machines to calculate distance and is the basis for accurate imaging.

exam1.question: What control adjusts the brightness of echoes returning from deeper structures?
exam1.explanation: Time Gain Compensation (TGC) selectively amplifies echoes returning from deeper structures to compensate for attenuation. This creates a more uniform image brightness at all depths.

exam1.question: Which type of resolution refers to the ability to distinguish two structures lying perpendicular to the beam?
exam1.explanation: Lateral resolution (also called azimuthal resolution) is the ability to distinguish two structures that are side-by-side, perpendicular to the ultrasound beam. It is determined by beam width.

exam1.question: What does the Doppler effect measure in ultrasound?
exam1.explanation: The Doppler effect measures the frequency shift that occurs when ultrasound reflects off moving structures (typically blood cells). This shift is proportional to the velocity of the moving target and is used to assess blood flow.

exam1.question: What is acoustic impedance?

options.text: The resistance of tissue to ultrasound propagation
The speed of sound in tissue
The frequency of the ultrasound beam
The power output of the transducer

exam1.explanation: Acoustic impedance is the resistance that tissue offers to the propagation of ultrasound. It is the product of tissue density and the speed of sound in that tissue. Differences in acoustic impedance between tissues create reflections.

exam1.question: What artifact appears as an anechoic shadow behind highly attenuating structures?
exam1.explanation: Acoustic shadowing appears as a dark (anechoic) area behind structures that strongly attenuate or reflect ultrasound, such as bone, calcifications, or gallstones. This occurs because little to no sound energy passes through to deeper structures.

exam1.question: Which transducer type produces a rectangular image format?
exam1.explanation: Linear array transducers produce a rectangular image format with uniform width throughout the image. They are commonly used for vascular imaging, musculoskeletal imaging, and small parts.

exam1.question: What happens to penetration as frequency increases?
exam1.explanation: As frequency increases, penetration decreases. Higher frequency sound waves are attenuated more rapidly in tissue, limiting their ability to penetrate deeply. This is why lower frequencies are used for imaging deeper structures.

exam1.question: What does the overall gain control adjust?

options.text: Brightness of the entire image uniformly

exam1.explanation: Overall gain adjusts the amplification of all returning echoes uniformly, affecting the brightness of the entire image equally at all depths. This is different from TGC, which selectively adjusts gain at different depths.

exam1.question: What is the primary advantage of harmonic imaging?

options.text: Improved image quality and reduced artifacts

exam1.explanation: Harmonic imaging uses frequency components generated within tissue (usually at twice the transmitted frequency). This technique reduces artifacts, improves contrast resolution, and produces cleaner images, especially in difficult-to-image patients.

exam2.question: What is the optimal Doppler angle for accurate velocity measurements?
exam2.explanation: The optimal Doppler angle is between 45-60 degrees. At 0 degrees, maximum Doppler shift is obtained but it may be difficult to position. At 90 degrees, no Doppler shift occurs. 60 degrees provides a good compromise between Doppler shift magnitude and beam-to-flow angle.

exam2.question: What causes aliasing in pulsed wave Doppler?
exam2.explanation: Aliasing occurs when the velocity of blood flow exceeds the Nyquist limit (half the pulse repetition frequency). This causes the Doppler waveform to wrap around and appear on the opposite side of the baseline, creating ambiguous velocity information.

exam2.question: Which artifact appears as bright echoes behind fluid-filled structures?
exam2.explanation: Acoustic enhancement (also called through-transmission) appears as increased echogenicity (brightness) behind fluid-filled structures. This occurs because fluid attenuates sound less than surrounding tissue, allowing more energy to reach deeper structures.

exam2.question: What is the mechanical index (MI) used to assess?
exam2.explanation: The Mechanical Index (MI) is used to assess the potential for non-thermal bioeffects, specifically cavitation. Cavitation is the formation and collapse of gas bubbles in tissue due to the mechanical pressure of ultrasound waves.

exam2.question: What is axial resolution dependent upon?
exam2.explanation: Axial resolution (also called longitudinal or range resolution) is the ability to distinguish two structures along the beam axis. It is determined by spatial pulse length - shorter pulses (fewer cycles, higher frequency) provide better axial resolution.
